title: Pallet racking and stored-load instability
audience: Cleaners who work near pallet racking and stored goods in a warehouse.
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of racking damage and unstable stored loads.
Keep clear of racking and loads that look unstable, and do not touch them.
Report the condition at once and stop work in the area.

instruction.heading: What you are looking at
instruction.body: A pallet racking system is a frame that holds stock in bays. The main parts are the upright frames that carry the load down to the floor, the horizontal beams that the pallets sit on, the diagonal and horizontal braces that stop the frame racking sideways, the connectors that join beams to uprights, the safety clips that stop beams lifting out of their connectors, and the floor fixings that anchor the frame. Each part is designed to carry a rated load. When one part is damaged, the rated load of the whole bay can fall, and the stored goods above a walkway can come down on whoever is below. A cleaner rarely knows the rated load of a bay, so the working rule is simple: if a bay looks wrong, treat it as unsafe until the site's competent person says otherwise.

instruction.heading: Recognising damage
instruction.body: Damage can be seen from the floor if you know what to look for. State regulator guidance on racking lists several common signs. Beam connectors that have bent into a V shape can point to overloading. Impact marks on beams from a pallet or forklift, and cracked welds, are another sign. Missing connectors and missing safety clips leave a beam free to lift out. A beam resting on only one end connector has popped out of its upright. Uprights that are twisted, split, cracked or badly spliced need attention, and so do bent braces. A frame that is out of plumb, meaning it leans away from the vertical, can result from impact, overloading or settlement in the floor. Damaged or missing floor fixings and a capacity sign that can no longer be read are further signs. On the load side, look for goods that overhang the pallet, pallets that are unstable or unlevel, goods that are not secured, loads that touch uprights or beams, and bays carrying more than their rated load. A load that leans over a walkway, or a pallet that sags in the middle, is an immediate concern rather than a tidy-up task.

instruction.heading: Keep clear, do not test, and use your right to stop
instruction.body: Do not climb, push, lean on or touch the racking or the stock to find out whether it is safe. Testing is the wrong method because a load that moves under a push can fall, and a frame that flexes may already be past its limit. Move out of the zone below and beside the damaged area, and keep other people out. Under the Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act 2011, a worker who has a reasonable concern about an immediate or imminent serious risk to their health or safety may cease or refuse unsafe work (Work Health and Safety Act 2011, section 84, compilation dated 1 July 2024). State versions of the law may differ, so check the one that applies on your site. The right to stop is a right to stop your own work and to withdraw from the area. It is not a right to repair the rack, move stock, or decide that the area is safe.

instruction.heading: Close, report and record
instruction.body: Once you have moved clear, close the area with barriers or signs, following the site's method, and tell your supervisor straight away. State guidance says employees must report racking damage immediately so that a competent person can assess it. Where the site uses a tagging system for damaged bays, follow the site procedure, but do not classify the damage yourself. Your report should name the aisle, bay and level, describe what you saw, say when you saw it, and state who you told and what they said. If the site allows photographs, take them from outside the danger zone without touching the rack. Keep the restriction in place until the site confirms in writing that the area can be used again.

instruction.heading: Who decides and what happens next
instruction.body: Formal racking inspections are carried out by a competent person at intervals of no more than 12 months, and a competent person should inspect racking that shows signs of overloading. State guidance says that very serious damage should lead to the affected bays being unloaded before reuse, and that changes to a rack should be made only by the supplier, their representative or a suitably competent person. Employers and workers should not modify uprights, bracing or beams, for example by welding on extra cleats, and replacement parts should come from the equipment manufacturer. A cleaner does not re-stack stock, move a damaged beam, decide that a rack is safe because it has stood for years, or approve a bay for loading. Those decisions belong to the site and its authorised people.

instruction.heading: Cleaning near racking in practice
instruction.body: Before you start an aisle, look up and along the bays for the signs listed above. Keep cleaning tools, mop buckets and vacuum hoses clear of the bases of uprights, because repeated knocks weaken frames. Do not use ladders, steps or shelving to reach a high surface near racking unless the site has authorised that task. Keep out of the zone where forklifts are working, and follow the site's traffic management plan. Where a walkway has a damaged bay above it, do not clean underneath until the site has dealt with the bay. Plan the work so the cleaning route can be moved if a bay is closed.

instruction.heading: The limits of this lesson
instruction.body: Completing this lesson does not make you a racking inspector, a rigger or a specialist, and it does not give any licence, certificate or authority to inspect, repair, re-stack or approve racking. Those tasks are done by authorised or competent people under the site's procedure. This lesson teaches you to recognise a warning sign, keep clear, stop, and report.

procedure: Before starting an aisle, look along the bays for bent uprights, torn or bent bracing, displaced or popped beams, missing connectors or clips, and leaning or overhanging loads.
If any sign is present, keep clear of the bay and the load. Do not climb, push, lean on or touch the racking or the stock.
Move out of the zone below and beside the damage, and keep other people out. Close the area with barriers or signs as the site method requires.
Tell the supervisor straight away and do not restart work in the area until they confirm it is safe.
Record the aisle, bay and level, the signs seen, the time, and who was told and what they said.
Wait for the site's competent person to inspect, unload, repair or re-stack. Do not do those tasks yourself.
Resume only on written confirmation from the site that the area has been released.

workedExamples.situation: A pallet load leans noticeably over the walkway you need to clean, and an upright in the same bay looks bent.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you not do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Keep clear of the leaning load and the bent upright. Do not push the load back or try to straighten the upright. Stop work in the walkway, keep people out, and report the bent upright and the leaning load to the supervisor at once, giving the aisle, bay and level and the time. Do not clean under the load while it is waiting for the site's response. The decision to unload, repair or re-stack belongs to the site.

workedExamples.situation: On a morning round you see a beam connector bent into a V shape in a bay that you normally clean around, and a pallet beam has a dent where a forklift hit it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the cleaning route still go ahead as planned?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A bent connector and an impact mark on a beam are both recognised warning signs, so the bay is not safe to work under until the site has assessed it. Keep the route clear, tell the supervisor, and ask for the bay to be assessed before you return. Reschedule the cleaning of that walkway to a time when the site confirms it is released, and record the reschedule so that the gap in the clean is explained.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor asks you to re-stack a few pallets in a bay that has a missing safety clip, so that the cleaning can be finished quickly.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Re-stacking a bay that is already showing a warning sign moves a load on a frame that may be damaged. Explain that re-stacking and the decision about the missing clip belong to the site's authorised person. Report the missing clip and the request, and keep clear until the authorised person has acted. Record that the request was made and that you did not carry it out.

equipmentAndPpe: High-visibility clothing and safety footwear, as the site requires.
Barriers, cones or signs for closing an aisle or walkway.
Hard hat where the site's risk assessment requires one for areas below racking.
A torch for checking the upper faces of beams and connectors from a safe distance.
Damage report form or site incident app, with aisle, bay and level fields.
A radio or phone to reach the supervisor straight away.
Camera, if the site allows photographs taken from outside the danger zone.

commonErrors.error: Pushing a leaning load back to check whether it will hold.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not touch the load. Stop, keep clear, and report it.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning directly under a damaged bay while the report is pending.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop work below the bay and keep people out until the site releases the area.

commonErrors.error: Deciding a rack is safe because it has stood for years or has never fallen.
commonErrors.prevention: Only the site's competent person decides. Age and history are not a safety assessment.

commonErrors.error: Re-stacking stock or straightening a beam to tidy the bay.
commonErrors.prevention: Re-stacking and repairs are not cleaning tasks. Report the condition and wait for the authorised person.

commonErrors.error: Reporting verbally and not recording the location or time.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the aisle, bay, level, signs, time and the person told on the report form.

commonErrors.error: Pulling a damage tag off a bay or moving a barrier to get past.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave tags and barriers in place. Ask the supervisor if the route has to change.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Commonwealth WHS law (section 84) lets a worker cease or refuse unsafe work where they have a reasonable concern about an immediate or imminent serious risk to their health or safety. This is a right to stop, not a right to repair.

State regulator guidance on pallet racking (checked 2026-11-03) says damage should be reported immediately, that formal inspections by a competent person should happen at intervals of no more than 12 months, and that racking should not be modified by unauthorised people. This guidance is not itself the law. Check the rules that apply in the state where the warehouse operates.

Racking inspection, repair, unloading and re-stacking are work for authorised or competent people. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval, rigging authority or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.
Traffic management, forklift separation and the standard for racking inspection on each site (including any reference to AS 4084) were not sourced for this lesson.

qualityStandard: Every warning sign present in a sample racking photograph is identified, with none missed.
In the case study, work below the damaged bay is stopped, the area is closed, and no contact is made with the racking or the stock.
The report gives the aisle, bay, level, signs, time and the person told, and the restriction stays in place until released in writing.
documentationEvidence: Racking and load condition report with aisle, bay, level, signs observed, time and the person notified.
Restriction record for the walkway, with the time it was closed and the written release from the site.
Record of any request to move stock or re-stack, showing that the request was passed on and not carried out.
summary: Recognise the signs of racking damage and unstable loads: bent, torn, displaced, missing or leaning parts.
Keep clear, do not touch or test the rack or the load, and stop work below the damage.
Report at once with location and time, and leave repair, unloading and re-stacking to the authorised person.

knowledgeChecks.question: A load leans over a walkway and an upright is bent. What is correct?
options: Push the load back into line with the upright
Stop work below, keep people out, and report
Clean quickly underneath before anyone notices

knowledgeChecks.question: Who decides whether racking is safe to use?
options: Any worker on the floor today

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is a warning sign of racking damage?
options: A torn bracing or a bent upright
A fresh coat of paint on the frame
A clean floor under the racking

knowledgeChecks.question: How often does state guidance say a formal racking inspection by a competent person should happen?
options: Only after a collision with a forklift
At intervals of no more than 12 months
Every five years, regardless of use
